## RESULTS

### CCC-RISE framework overview

::: {#fig-1}
![](figures/figure1/figure1.svg){width="6.5in"}

**CCC-RISE deconvolves variation in cell communication across single cells and conditions.** ({{< panel 1 workflow.1 >}}) RISE projects multi-condition scRNA-seq data into eigen-states and decomposes the resulting condition by eigen-state by gene tensor.
({{< panel 1 workflow.2 >}}) Communication scores are then computed between eigen-states for ligand--receptor (LR) pairs to form a 4D communication tensor.
({{< panel 1 workflow.3 >}}) CPD decomposes the communication tensor into factors that describe the component associations with conditions, sender eigen-states, receiver eigen-states, and LR pairs.
({{< panel 1 component-interpretation >}}) Each CCC-RISE component represents a communication program defined by the association weights across four dimensions: sender cells, receiver cells, LR pairs, and experimental conditions.
({{< panel 1 cell-mapping >}}) Sender and receiver eigen-state factors are mathematically combined with the RISE projections to map communication patterns back to specific single-cell populations.
({{< panel 1 embedding >}}) RISE projections serve as a common embedding basis to visualize cell-to-cell heterogeneity across all conditions.
:::

RISE projects cells from multiple conditions onto a common reference frame, effectively aligning them based on gene expression without requiring *a priori* labeling \ [@doi:10.1016/j.cels.2025.101294].
RISE then factorizes the resulting tensor into components representing patterns of variation across conditions, eigen-states, and genes ({{< fig 1 workflow.1 >}}).
To overcome the limitations of aggregating data into pre-defined cell types CCC-RISE infers communication directly from RISE's unsupervised eigen-states rather than individual cells or broad populations.
For every experimental condition and ligand--receptor (LR) pair---defined using CellChat's reference database---a score is calculated for all combinations of sender and receiver eigen-states by integrating the ligand expression of the sender with the receptor expression of the receiver [@doi:10.1038/s41467-021-21246-9].
We elected to score LR communication by taking the product of their expression values, the simplest, most fundamental of the many available continuous CCC scoring methods [@doi:10.1038/s41576-020-00292-x].
This process yields a four-dimensional tensor describing the data across sender eigen-states, receiver eigen-states, experimental conditions, and LR pairs ({{< fig 1 workflow.2 >}}).

To extract patterns from this high-dimensional structure, CCC-RISE employs Canonical Polyadic Decomposition (CPD), which decomposes the 4D tensor into distinct components ({{< fig 1 workflow.3 >}}).
Akin to principal component analysis (PCA), this decomposition approximates the tensor as a sum of rank-one tensors, each representing a communication program defined by specific variation in conditions, sender and receiver states, and LR pairs ({{< fig 1 component-interpretation >}})\ [@doi:10.1137/07070111X; @doi:10.1016/j.cels.2024.07.004; @doi:10.1007/0-306-47815-3_5].
Crucially, because the original RISE projections preserve cell-to-cell heterogeneity, the component loadings on eigen-states can be projected back onto individual cells.
By multiplying the RISE projections with the sender and receiver eigen-state factors, the specific associations of individual cells with each communication component are recovered ({{< fig 1 cell-mapping >}}).
This enables the tracing of signaling programs across conditions without losing the granularity of the underlying single-cell data ({{< fig 1 embedding >}}).

## CCC-RISE isolates subpopulation-specific repair signaling in lung transplants

::: {#fig-2}
![](figures/figure2/figure2.svg){width="6.5in"}

**CCC-RISE identifies stable communication programs among epithelial subpopulations.** ({{< panel 2 rise-rank-selection >}}) RISE R^2^X across ranks of the fit on all data and, in BiCV, of the fit on the training block (BiCV train) and its prediction of the held-out block (BiCV test); mean ± SD over 10 repeats.
({{< panel 2 cp-rank-selection.1 >}}) CP fit R^2^X and aggregate imputation R^2^X of held-out entries over 10 folds across ranks (mean ± SD over three replicates per rank).
({{< panel 2 cp-rank-selection.2 >}}) The largest number of modes in which any pair of CP components is collinear (\|cosine\| > 0.9), marked as near-duplicate or opposite-signed (cancelling) pairs, across ranks.
({{< panel 2 aggregate-fms >}}) Aggregate FMS of RISE and CP factors across leave-one-patient-out jackknife (n = 45) and re-initialization (n = 47) replicates; bars show the 2.5th--97.5th percentiles.
({{< panel 2 cp-factor-matrices >}}) CP factor matrices representing component loadings of conditions, sender/receiver eigen-states, and LR pairs.
({{< panel 2 permutation-lr-significance.1 >}}) Fraction of each LR pair's (n = 513) condition by sender by receiver entries exceeding a null of 1,000 within-sample cell permutations at p < 0.05.
p is the fraction of permuted scores at least as large as the observed score, (k + 1)/(1,000 + 1) for k permutations.
({{< panel 2 permutation-lr-significance.2 >}}) Mean observed against mean permuted communication score per LR pair, colored by fraction of entries significant.
({{< panel 2 nichenet >}}) Ligand-weighted mean NicheNet target-score of each component's ligands (diamonds) against the same mean on 1,000 copies of the NicheNet v2 ligand--target prior with shuffled gene--ligand links.
Boxes show the quartiles and whiskers show the 2.5th--97.5th percentiles.
\*: q < 0.05; n.s.: q ≥ 0.05; one-sided permutation test, Benjamini--Hochberg corrected across the five components.
({{< panel 2 sender-receiver-strata >}}) Per-cell component 5 sender against receiver weight.
Cells above 30% of either weight's maximum form the sender or receiver group, assigned by the larger relative weight.
({{< panel 2 epithelial-markers >}}) Expression of canonical epithelial subtype markers and top LR pair genes in each group.
Markers were curated from Travaglini et al.\ and Sikkema et al.\ [@doi:10.1038/s41586-020-2922-4; @doi:10.1038/s41591-023-02327-2].
({{< panel 2 celltype-composition >}}) Annotated cell-type composition of each group.
:::

We applied CCC-RISE to 47 bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) samples from 45 lung transplant recipients, of which 17 were stable controls and 30 had acute lung allograft dysfunction (ALAD) ({{< fig alad-cohort cohort >}})\ [@doi:10.1016/j.healun.2024.02.007].
ALAD is an acute decline in lung function following transplantation that either resolves or progresses to chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD), a largely irreversible loss of graft function that leads to re-transplantation or death\ [@doi:10.1016/j.trre.2021.100626; @doi:10.1016/j.healun.2022.05.005].
Our ALAD cohort was composed of broad immune and epithelial cell types whose proportional abundances did not differ significantly between control, declined, and recovered samples ({{< fig alad-cohort celltype-proportions >}}).
We used this cohort to establish how a CCC-RISE model is selected, validated, and interpreted.

We first selected the RISE rank by bi-cross-validation (BiCV), which fits RISE to a random half of all cells and genes and scores the fit's ability to predict the held-out block of cells and genes\ [@doi:10.1214/08-AOAS227].
Held-out R^2^X rose steeply, plateaued around rank 10, and reached its maximum at rank 17, which we used to construct the communication tensor ({{< fig 2 rise-rank-selection >}}, {{< fig rise-factor-matrices >}}).
Seeking a similarly definitive rank-selection criterion for CP, we evaluated the reconstruction and imputation accuracy (i.e., the accuracy the outer product of CP factors in approximating either the original communication tensor or entries held out during fitting, respectively) of CP models at varying ranks.
Both CP fit R^2^X and imputation R^2^X generally increased with rank, indicating that higher-rank CP models did not lose predictive accuracy ({{< fig 2 cp-rank-selection.1 >}}).
However, neither reconstruction metric provided a clear choice for CP rank, so we instead computed the cosine similarity between components at each rank, a measurement of collinearity and degeneracy.
A pair of components first became collinear in two modes with opposing signs at rank 6, and every subsequent rank contained a pair collinear in at least two modes.
In contrast, ranks 3--5 produced only one pair of components overlapping in a single mode, as expected when programs share a sender or receiver population.
We therefore selected CP rank 5 as the lowest rank before the model became degenerate ({{< fig 2 cp-rank-selection.2 >}}).

We next asked whether the communication programs captured by CCC-RISE were stable, exceeded chance, and aligned with external biological validation.
RISE and CP components were stable over re-initialization (aggregate FMS 1.000) and leave-one-patient-out jackknife (aggregate FMS 0.985 for RISE, 0.999 for CP) ({{< fig 2 aggregate-fms >}}, {{< fig cmp-stability >}}).
To assess robustness, we extended the cluster-label permutation of CellPhoneDB and CellChat to continuous eigen-states by shuffling which cell's expression is paired with each eigen-state projection and recomputing the communication tensor\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-021-21246-9; @doi:10.1038/s41596-020-0292-x].
Per LR pair, a median of 9.7% of entries exceeded this null at p < 0.05 and mean observed scores exceeded mean null scores for 99% of LR pairs ({{< fig 2 permutation-lr-significance >}}).
Finally, we tested whether each component's receiver cells showed transcriptional evidence of ligand signaling by scoring how well differential expression (DE) in the component's top receiver cells recovered each ligand's NicheNet-predicted downstream gene targets ({{< fig nichenet ligand-scores >}})\ [@doi:10.1038/s41592-019-0667-5; @doi:10.1038/s41596-024-01121-9].
Averaged with each ligand's weight in the component, ligand target-score percentiles exceeded those obtained with randomly reassigned ligand--target links for components 3--5 (q < 0.05) ({{< fig 2 nichenet >}}, {{< fig nichenet weighted-percentiles >}}).
Thus, the receiver cells of components 3--5 upregulate the downstream targets of the ligands these components weight most heavily.

RISE eigen-states allow cellular identity to be traced from CP component weights back to single-cell gene expression without depending on prior annotations.
We illustrate this with component 5, whose sender and receiver loadings were spread across several eigen-states ({{< fig 2 cp-factor-matrices.2 cp-factor-matrices.3 >}}, {{< fig cmp5-identity eigenstate-scatter cmp-eigenstate-loadings >}}), suggesting signaling between populations.
Combining these loadings with each cell's RISE projections gave per-cell sender and receiver weights, which few cells carried simultaneously; thresholding them defined 67 sender and 58 receiver cells ({{< fig 2 sender-receiver-strata >}}).
We found that these groups both expressed canonical epithelial marker genes (FXYD3, EPCAM, and ELF3) at significantly higher levels relative to cells with low component 5 weight ({{< fig cmp5-identity celltype-markers group-vs-rest >}}).
Individually, the groups expressed unique epithelial subpopulation markers indicating communication between ciliated sender cells and basal/secretory receiver cells ({{< fig 2 epithelial-markers >}}, {{< fig cmp5-identity sender-vs-receiver >}}).
These eigen-state--derived epithelial labels closely aligned with available annotations while exceeding their granularity in epithelial subtype definitions ({{< fig 2 celltype-composition >}}).
In sum, label-free interpretation of CCC-RISE factors isolated a well-validated CCC program, wherein ciliated epithelial cells secrete betacellulin (BTC) that binds basal and secretory epithelial cells through epidermal growth factor receptors EGFR and ErbB2, inducing tissue repair and---in unhealthy tissue---fibrosis ({{< fig 2 cp-factor-matrices.4 >}})\ [@doi:10.1165/ajrcmb.20.5.3308; @doi:10.1038/ki.2012.43; @doi:10.3390/cells11060986].

## A coordinated immune communication axis is associated with ALAD outcomes

::: {#fig-3}
![](figures/figure3/figure3.svg){width="6.5in"}

**CCC-RISE identifies a coordinated immune signaling axis associated with ALAD outcomes.** ({{< panel 3 outcome-association >}}) CP component 4 condition loadings by six-month outcome: no CLAD (n = 21), recovered (n = 12), CLAD (n = 12), and died (n = 2).
Lines connect samples from the same patient.
Boxes show the median and interquartile range and whiskers show the most extreme values within 1.5× the interquartile range.
One-way ANOVA F and η^2^, with Benjamini--Hochberg correction across all outcomes and components ({{< fig alad-associations cp-associations >}}).
({{< panel 3 celltype-association >}}) Mean per-cell sender and receiver weight of each annotated cell type on each CP component; component 4 is outlined.
({{< panel 3 lr-loadings >}}) CP component 4 LR pair loadings against their rank, with the top 10 LR pairs labeled.
({{< panel 3 coordinated-changes.1 >}}) ANOVA η^2^ of each LR pair's (n = 513) communication scores with six-month outcome.
Association strengths of component 4's top 10 LR pairs and its condition loadings are marked.
({{< panel 3 coordinated-changes.2 >}}) Spearman correlation across conditions between each pair of component 4's top 10 LR pairs and between pairs drawn 2,000 times from the remaining LR pairs: at random, matched in expression (each from the 20 pairs nearest a top pair in log mean score), or among the other LR pairs associated with six-month outcome (q < 0.05).
Boxes show the median and interquartile range, and whiskers show the most extreme values within 1.5× the interquartile range.
({{< panel 3 lr-permutation >}}) Diamonds: Difference in mean communication score between CLAD/died and no-CLAD samples (n = 14 and 33 samples) of each of component 4's top 10 LR pairs.
Violins: Null differences across 10,000 permutations of outcome labels between patients.
All results are normalized by standard deviations of the null.
q: one-sided permutation p, Benjamini--Hochberg corrected across the 10 pairs.
({{< panel 3 lr-volcano >}}) Log~2~ ratio of mean communication score in CLAD/died to no-CLAD samples against one-sided permutation p for each CP component's top 20 LR pairs by loading; component 4's top 10 pairs are labeled where p < 0.05.
:::

Having demonstrated CCC-RISE's capacity to resolve subpopulation heterogeneity, we next asked whether CCC-RISE components were associated with clinical outcome.
ANOVA of each component's condition loadings against patient outcomes revealed three outcomes significantly associated with CP component 4 after multiple-test correction: six-month outcome, comprising no CLAD, recovered, CLAD, and died groups, and six-month and one-year death ({{< fig 3 outcome-association >}}, {{< fig alad-associations cp-associations >}}, {{< panel alad-associations death-weights >}}).
The same test applied to the condition loadings of RISE components yielded no significant associations, suggesting that the outcome association emerged only once gene expression was organized into intercellular communication ({{< fig alad-associations rise-associations >}}).
Mapping component 4's sender and receiver loadings onto annotated cell labels revealed signaling among CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and natural killer (NK) cells ({{< fig 3 celltype-association >}}).
Per-cell sender and receiver weights on component 4 were nearly identical (R^2^ = 0.98), indicating that the same cells were acting as both senders and receivers of component 4 signals ({{< fig alad-associations sender-receiver-scatter >}}).
Component 4's top LR pairs consisted of markers of immune cell activation/exhaustion (GZMA--F2R, ADORA2A--ENTPD1, and NECTIN3--TIGIT), immune-activating chemokines and receptors (CCL4/CCL5--CCR4/CCR5 and CXCL13--CXCR3), and activating co-stimulatory ligands and receptors (CD70--CD27 and TNFSF4--TNFRSF4) ({{< fig 2 cp-factor-matrices.4 >}}, {{< fig 3 lr-loadings >}}).
CP component 4 thus collectively represents an inflammatory communication axis within activated immune populations that is upregulated in CLAD-positive and deceased patients.

CPD groups LR pairs based on covariation across conditions, senders, and receivers rather than by their association with outcome.
Indeed, while some of component 4's top LR pairs exhibited strong individual association with outcome, they were not the only highly associated LR pairs and were not defined as a group by their ability to stratify patients ({{< fig 3 coordinated-changes.1 >}}).
Individual outcome association therefore did not explain which LR pairs component 4 grouped together.
Instead, component 4's top LR pairs were more strongly correlated with one another across conditions than randomly drawn LR pairs, LR pairs matched in mean communication score, or other LR pairs significantly associated with outcome ({{< fig 3 coordinated-changes.2 >}}).
The expression-matched baseline excludes shared abundance as the source of this coordination, and the outcome-associated baseline shows that it is not explained by a common association with outcome.
These results indicate that, by modeling variation across conditions, cells, and LR pairs together, CCC-RISE isolates coordinated communication programs from sets of individual communication axes with equal or greater clinical association.

Given the limited size of the ALAD cohort, we tested whether the component 4 association could be explained by patient covariates, individual patients, or patient grouping.
No patient covariate was associated with six-month outcome or six-month death, even without multiple-test correction, while Caucasian ethnicity was weakly associated with one-year death ({{< fig alad-associations covariates >}}).
The six-month outcome association remained significant in 44 of 45 leave-one-patient-out jackknife replicates ({{< fig anova-stability effect-size-distributions significant-fraction >}}).
The one exception left out one of the two patients who died within six months, whose sample carried the highest component 4 condition loading.
We next applied scDiffCom's condition-label--permutation scheme to our communication tensor to test whether each LR pair's difference in communication score between CLAD/died and no-CLAD samples exceeded those obtained with permuted patient outcome labels\ [@doi:10.1038/s43587-023-00514-x].
Eight of component 4's ten top LR pairs had significantly higher communication scores in CLAD/died samples than in no-CLAD samples, indicating that communication scores constructed through RISE exceeded chance in their ability to stratify patients ({{< fig 3 lr-permutation lr-volcano >}}).

Choice of CCC scoring method used to construct the communication tensor is a known source of disagreement between tools, so we asked whether component 4 was an artifact of CCC-RISE's communication score\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-022-30755-0].
We compared four approaches used to convert expression to LR interaction scores: product, used by CCC-RISE, Tensor-cell2cell, and NATMI\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-022-31369-2; @doi:10.1038/s41467-020-18873-z]; mean, used by CellPhoneDB\ [@doi:10.1038/s41596-020-0292-x]; geometric mean (gmean), used by scDiffCom\ [@doi:10.1038/s43587-023-00514-x]; and Hill function, used by CellChat\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-021-21246-9].
Upon recomputing the communication tensor from a single RISE fit using each scoring method, we observed that each alternate score generally yielded a CP fit closely matching that of CCC-RISE's product ({{< fig ccc-scoring factor-match >}}).
Further, the recovered component remained associated with six-month outcome under every score, although the mean and gmean scores also associated component 3 with outcome ({{< fig ccc-scoring anova >}}).
The alternate scores captured LR pairs similar to those of the product score, especially in components 4 and 5 ({{< fig ccc-scoring interpretation.1 >}}).
For component 4, every score identified T and NK cells as senders, and the Hill score identified the same cells as receivers, whereas the mean and gmean scores instead implicated epithelial receivers ({{< fig ccc-scoring interpretation.2 >}}).
Overall, CCC-RISE's expression product agreed closely with CellChat's expression Hill function, and even lower-FMS scores closely matched the LR pairs and either the sender or receiver eigen-states of components 4 and 5.

## Distinct CD4+ T cell and NK cell signaling programs define ALAD

Having demonstrated CCC-RISE\'s capacity to resolve subpopulation heterogeneity, we next evaluated its generalizability in a clinically distinct setting.
We applied the framework to BAL samples from lung transplant recipients to distinguish patients with acute lung allograft dysfunction (ALAD) from stable controls (Fig. 4a).
ALAD patients have a significant drop (10% decrease) in FEV₁ (a measure of forced exhalation) and worsening oxygenation, leading to rapid lung function decline after transplantation and denoting concern for the onset of chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD)\ [@doi:10.1016/j.healun.2024.02.015; @doi:10.1016/j.trre.2021.100626; @doi:10.1016/j.healun.2022.08.012].
The immune mechanisms driving this injury remain poorly understood\ [@doi:10.1016/j.healun.2025.04.015].
Our cohort included a broad composition of immune and epithelial cell types; notably, there were no significant differences in the proportional abundance of these populations between ALAD and control patients, suggesting that the pathology is driven by altered communication rather than simple changes in cell numbers (Supplementary Fig. 5a).
We optimized the CCC-RISE model using cross-validation and logistic regression, determining that a decomposition into 15 RISE eigen-states and 18 CPD components yielded the optimal predictive performance for ALAD status (Fig. 4b-c).
The factors demonstrated high stability (Supplementary Fig. 5b-e) and effectively resolved distinct cell types within a common embedding space across all samples (Fig. 4f, Supplementary Fig. 5f).

The logistic regression analysis identified three primary components that strongly discriminated between patient groups: Component 5 was associated with ALAD status, while Components 13 and 17 were associated with control samples (Fig. 4d).
These associations remained robust even when analyzing pairwise combinations of components, indicating they represent stable biological signals (Supplementary Fig. 5g).
The model successfully captured distinct communication programs for each component, defined by specific weights across LR pairs and cell populations (Fig. 4e, Supplementary Figs. 5h, 6, and 7).

Investigating the ALAD-associated signal, Component 5 was characterized by a specific interaction between CD4+ T cells and dendritic cells (DCs) (Fig. 4g-h).
This program was dominated by CD40LG-CD40 signaling, which exhibited a much stronger interaction profile and weighting compared to other pairs like LTA-LTBR (Fig. 4e, i-j).
Crucially, the communication scores for this interaction revealed considerable heterogeneity within the CD4+ T cell and DC populations, confirming that the signal is driven by specific active subsets rather than the total population.
Examining the transcriptional signature of CD4+ T cells with greater communication revealed features suggestive of regulatory T cells (FOXP3, TNFRSF25) with stem-like features (SELL, LEF1) participating in lymphoid-like structures (LTA; Fig. 4k).

In contrast, Components 13 and 17 defined distinct signaling networks associated with stable control patients.
Component 13 was driven primarily by interactions between DCs and epithelial cells (Fig. 4l-o).
The top-weighted LR pairs for this component included CD200-CD200R1 and IL27-related interactions, which were distinct from those found in other components (Fig. 4e, Supplementary Fig. 5i).
Communication scores highlighted a prominent role for DCs and epithelial cells in this potentially protective program, particularly via the CD200-CD200R1 axis (Fig. 4p).
DCs with greater sender activity had features of Langerhans cells (CD207, CD1A, CD1E, CD301), while epithelial cells with greater receiver activity had associations with a unique differentiation program (e.g. KRT4, DSP, MMP10) (Fig. 4q-r).
Finally, Component 17 revealed a separate control-associated program involving NK cells and CD8+ T cells (Fig. 4s-t).
This component was heavily weighted toward the GZMA-F2R interaction (Fig. 4e), with single-cell resolution analysis confirming that this signaling axis is actively utilized by both NK and CD8+ T cell populations in stable grafts (Fig. 4u-v).
High communication NK cells were enriched for other transcriptional features associated with activation and cytotoxicity, such as FASLG and 2B4, while the high receiving CD8+ T cells showed other markers of activation, such as CTLA4 and CLIC3 (Fig. 4w-x).

Having defined the cellular communication networks associated with ALAD, we sought to contextualize their broader clinical significance by comparing the identified CCC-RISE components against patient demographic and physiological variables.
We found no significant correlations between the components and variables such as sex, age, or FEV~1~ measured at 6 months and 1-year post-transplant (Supplementary Fig. 8a-b).
Beyond the initial ALAD diagnosis, we investigated whether these components could predict progression to CLAD or mortality, outcomes marked by continued functional decline\ [@doi:10.1016/j.healun.2024.02.015].
Our analysis revealed that the sample associations for these components showed no significant association with either CLAD or deceased status at 6 months and 1-year post-ALAD diagnosis as separate outcomes (Supplementary Fig. 8c-h).

Given these findings, we expanded our analysis to determine if other signatures from CCC-RISE could stratify patients based on their clinical trajectories, specifically distinguishing those who remained stable from those who experienced clinical decline leading to CLAD or death in aggregate.
Using the original factorization, we applied logistic regression to identify components predictive of these outcomes.
Components 7 and 17 emerged as significant predictors for stratifying patient stability (Fig. 5a).
Notably, the components differentiating stable status were consistently identified as significant when assessing pairwise interactions, even if they were potentially filtered out by L1 regularization in isolation (Supplementary Fig. 8i).

The analysis reaffirmed the importance of the GZMA-F2R and CCL5-F2R interactions within NK and CD8+ T cell populations as associated with better outcomes, this time stable lung function after ALAD.
These interactions were previously identified as predictors for control patients without ALAD, suggesting that the GZMA-F2R axis represents a consistent communication pathway in successful allografts, likely reflecting appropriate immune surveillance that avoids excessive inflammation.
Conversely, Component 7 was the most heavily weighted predictor of clinical decline, highlighting a distinct signal driven by CD4+ T cells (Fig. 5b-c).
The strongest ligand-receptor interactions included CD70-CD27 and LTA-TNFRSF1B (Fig. 5d).
Detailed analysis of CD4+ T cell communication patterns revealed that the CD70-CD27 interaction profile was substantially more robust than that of LTA-TNFRSF1B or other pairs (Fig. 5e-f).
Analysis of the distinguishing features of senders and receivers identified overlapping markers of activation (CAMK4, CLU; Fig. 5g-h).
This implicates the CD70-CD27 axis as a potential driver of pathological signaling associated with clinical deterioration.
CD70+ CD4+ T cells were similarly identified in an independent cohort of small airway brushings from recipients with stable allograft function or ALAD\ [@doi:10.1016/j.healun.2025.04.015].
Despite the limited sample size, the fraction of CD70+ CD4+ T cells were elevated in ALAD compared to stable controls (Supplementary Fig. S9).
